finding.title: Install always reports success, so callers can't detect or contain conflicts
finding.evidence: `return true;` is now unconditional, so the false return for conflicts in the spec is gone. Callers can no longer find or limit installs that overwrote non-link nodes.

finding.title: Redundant delete before assignment
finding.evidence: `delete fs[target]` is immediately followed by `fs[target]=...`, which already replaces the node, so the delete adds nothing. Restore the kind check instead.

finding.title: No test shows that a session cannot read another tenant's document by supplying a matching request.tenant
finding.evidence: The fixture includes no tests for the new behavior. A regression test with session.tenant='A', request.tenant='B' and row.tenant='B' that expects null would have caught this change.

finding.title: Unused request counter is left in place
finding.evidence: `++state.request` still runs, but nothing reads its value anymore. This makes it look like requests are still ordered when they aren't. Either restore the comparison (the correct fix) or remove the counter.

finding.title: Request counter is incremented but never read
finding.evidence: `++state.request` still runs, but nothing reads the value, so it suggests requests are ordered when they are not. The Product lens also called this dead code. The fix for the blocker (capture the id and compare it in the callback) resolves this too.

finding.title: No test covers multi-hop alias chains for the /repo guard
finding.evidence: The change includes no test showing that a chain of two or more aliases ending under /repo is refused and records no operation. A test like that would have caught this regression. Fix: go back to `resolved=canonical(path,links)`, use `resolved` in the push, and add tests for 0, 1 and 2+ hop chains plus the exact '/repo' boundary.

finding.title: Reads moved outside the snapshot and the transaction result is no longer returned
finding.evidence: The before code read balances with tx.get inside an isolated snapshot and returned the result of db.transaction. The after code reads with db.get outside any isolation, so concurrent transfers can read the same balance and overwrite each other's update. It also returns undefined, which breaks any caller that used the transaction's return value.

finding.title: Return value changed: transfer no longer returns the transaction result
finding.evidence: Before, transfer returned db.transaction(...). After, it returns undefined. Callers that await or check the result of transfer will see a different value than they used to.

finding.title: Reads and writes are no longer isolated, so concurrent transfers can lose updates
finding.evidence: db.get and db.save now run outside an isolated snapshot. If another transfer touches the same account between the get and the save, one of the updates is overwritten. Before, tx.get and tx.save ran inside the isolated transaction snapshot.

finding.title: Transfer result is no longer returned to callers
finding.evidence: The before code returned db.transaction(...), so callers got the commit result and could await it or see it fail. The after code returns undefined. Callers that rely on the return value to confirm or monitor the transfer lose that signal.

finding.title: Reads and writes now run outside the isolated snapshot, so concurrent transfers can lose updates
finding.evidence: Staff engineer and Data & contracts both reported this. The before code used tx.get/tx.save inside db.transaction, which the context describes as writing to an isolated snapshot. The after code uses db.get followed by db.save with no isolation. Two concurrent transfers on the same account can read the same balance, and one update can overwrite the other.

finding.title: transfer() no longer returns the transaction result
finding.evidence: Staff engineer, Data & contracts and Operability all reported this. Before, transfer returned `db.transaction(...)`. After, there is no return statement, so it returns undefined. Any caller that awaits or checks the result, or relies on it to see a failure, now gets different behaviour. The impact depends on what db.transaction returns, which the fixture does not specify.

finding.title: Reads and writes no longer use an isolated snapshot, so concurrent transfers can lose updates
finding.evidence: The old code read and wrote through tx, which works on an isolated snapshot. The new code calls db.get and then db.save directly, so it reads a value, changes it and writes it back with no isolation. Two transfers running at the same time can read the same balance, and one write will overwrite the other.

finding.title: Return value of transfer changed
finding.evidence: The old code returned the result of db.transaction(...), so callers could see whether the transfer committed. The new code returns undefined, which changes the function's contract for callers.

finding.title: Return contract changed: transfer no longer returns the transaction result
finding.evidence: Before, transfer returned the result of db.transaction(...). Now it returns undefined. Any caller that awaits or checks that result for commit status gets nothing back. Callers could also have relied on the transaction's outcome to detect a failure.

finding.title: Reads happen outside an isolated snapshot, so balances can be read stale or lost between get and save
finding.evidence: Before, tx.get read from an isolated snapshot. Now db.get and db.save run on live state with no isolation. If two transfers run at the same time on the same account, one can overwrite the other's update (a lost update), which corrupts the balance.

finding.title: transfer no longer returns the db.transaction result
finding.evidence: Before, transfer returned the result of db.transaction(...). Now it has no return statement, so it returns undefined. Any caller that uses the result loses it. The Staff engineer lens reported the same change, and Operability listed it as a gap. No callers were supplied, so the impact is not confirmed.

finding.title: No test covers focus restoration on Escape
finding.evidence: The change ships no test. A regression test should open with a mock trigger, send Escape, and assert `state.open===false` and `trigger.focus` was called once. It should also check that non-Escape keys do not close the dialog or move focus. The removed behavior would otherwise go unnoticed.

finding.title: Refactor changes the not-found return value when session.tenant is undefined
finding.evidence: Before, a falsy row always hit `return null`. After, `row?.tenant===session.tenant ? row : null` evaluates `undefined===undefined` as true when `find` returns undefined or null and `session.tenant` is undefined. The function then returns `row` (undefined) rather than null. This is not a leak, because no record is exposed. It does break the null-return contract on that path. Context says tenant IDs are opaque strings, so the case is unlikely. The optional chaining also made the tenant comparison harder to reason about than the explicit `!row` guard.

finding.title: No test covers the zero-cents boundary
finding.evidence: No tests come with the change. The spec singles out 0 vs null as the key distinction, and a test where `quote` returns 0 and expects `available: true` (plus a null case expecting false) would have caught this regression.

finding.title: No test covers the focus-restoration behavior
finding.evidence: The change deletes the only code that implements the spec'd behavior and adds no test. A test that opens with a mock trigger, sends Escape, and asserts `trigger.focus` was called once would have caught the regression. Non-Escape keys should also be covered, to confirm they leave the dialog open and do not move focus.

finding.title: No regression test covering the zero-cents boundary
finding.evidence: The change alters availability semantics, but no tests are supplied. The contract has three distinct cases: null, 0, and a positive integer. A test for `quote() === 0` expecting `available:true` would have caught this defect.

finding.title: No guard for out-of-range or stale selection
finding.evidence: archiveSelected dereferences rows[selection].id without checking that the row exists. An empty list, a filtered list, or a null selection throws instead of being a safe no-op.

finding.title: No tests for the new behavior
finding.evidence: No tests are supplied. The spec's key scenarios (archive after filter, archive after sort, stale selection) are uncovered. A test that selects a row, reorders the rows, and archives would have caught the regression.

finding.title: No test covers focus restoration on Escape
finding.evidence: The change removes the behavior the spec requires, and no test catches it. A test should call open(trigger), send onKey with {key:'Escape'}, and check that trigger.focus was called (or that document.activeElement === trigger after unmount). It should also check that keys other than Escape leave state.open true and don't move focus.

finding.title: Returns true on conflicts, breaking the spec's return-false contract
finding.evidence: The function now always runs `return true;`. Callers expect false when a real file or directory is in the way. Without that signal they cannot tell that a conflict happened, and they cannot know data was overwritten.

finding.title: The `delete` is unnecessary
finding.evidence: `delete fs[target]` comes right before an assignment that already replaces the whole node, so it does nothing useful and only makes the destructive intent more obvious. Restoring the original guard is the right fix. The delete is not needed.

finding.title: Leftover request counter increment has no purpose
finding.evidence: `++state.request;` still runs, but nothing reads the value any more. It looks like the ordering protection is still there when it is not. Restore the captured-token comparison and keep the increment.

finding.title: Request counter is still incremented but no longer used
finding.evidence: `++state.request;` is still there, but nothing reads its value any more. This makes it look like stale responses are still being handled when they aren't.

finding.title: Request counter is still incremented but nothing reads it
finding.evidence: Merged from the Staff engineer and Product reports. `++state.request;` still runs, but nothing reads the value, so it looks like stale responses are still handled when they aren't. The blocker fix resolves this too: restore the captured token and the comparison rather than deleting the increment.

finding.title: No test covers the retry bound
finding.evidence: The change touches the boundary but adds no test. A request stub that always returns retryable should assert exactly 3 calls and that the last response is returned. Other cases to cover are success on attempts 1, 2 and 3, and a non-retryable failure returning immediately. Any of these boundary tests would have caught the 4-call regression.

finding.title: No tests for cross-tenant access or for a spoofed request tenant
finding.evidence: The change swaps the trust boundary with no accompanying tests. Missing cases: session tenant matches and request tenant is absent or different (should return the row); session tenant differs while request.tenant is set to the document's tenant (should return null); and a missing row (should return null). Any of the first two would have caught this regression.

finding.title: Read-modify-write runs outside the isolated snapshot, so concurrent transfers can overwrite each other

finding.evidence: The old code returned db.transaction(...). The new code returns undefined, so any caller that awaits or chains on transfer() to learn whether the commit finished now gets nothing back.

finding.title: Out-of-range index after filtering throws or archives undefined
finding.evidence: If a filter shrinks `rows` below the stored index, `rows[selection]` is undefined, and `rows[selection].id` throws a TypeError. The archive action then fails for the user. Before the change, archive was called with the stored id and did not depend on the current rows.

finding.title: Archive throws a TypeError if a filter leaves fewer rows than the stored index
finding.evidence: Raised by Staff engineer, and also by Product inside its wrong-row finding. If a filter shortens `rows` so that its length is at or below the stored index, `rows[selection]` is undefined. Reading `.id` on it throws a TypeError, so archive fails for the user. The before code passed the stored id directly and did not depend on the current rows. Correction to the original title: the code never archives `undefined`. It throws before `archive` is called.

finding.title: No tests cover archiving after a filter or sort
finding.evidence: The spec explicitly requires archive to work after the list is filtered or reordered, but the change includes no tests for that. A test that selects a row, reorders or filters `rows`, then checks which id archive receives would catch the regression above. So would a test where the filtered list is shorter than the selected index.

finding.title: No tests for tenant isolation or spoofed request tenant
finding.evidence: The change alters the authorization logic and no tests are shown. Needed cases: a matching session tenant returns the row, a different session tenant returns null, and a spoofed request.tenant that differs from session.tenant returns null. A missing id and a missing request.tenant should also be covered. A test for the spoofed case would have caught this regression.

finding.title: Return value of transfer changed from the transaction result to undefined
finding.evidence: Before: `return db.transaction(...)` passed the transaction result to callers. After: transfer has no return statement, so callers that relied on the result, or awaited it if transaction is async, now get undefined.

finding.title: Primary submit button lost its explicit type attribute
finding.evidence: Before: button:{tag:'button',type:'submit',text:'Save'}. After: button:{tag:'button',text:'Save'}. Submission still works because a native button with omitted type defaults to submit inside a form, and the context states the form has exactly one primary button and no other submit handlers. finding.title: Explicit type removed; submit behavior relies on implicit default and no test covers it
finding.evidence: The change drops type:'submit' from the button. The context says native buttons with omitted type default to submit, and the form has one primary button and no other submit handlers. So click and Enter-in-input should still submit and call save once, and the spec is met. The risk is that the button is now less explicit. A renderer or a later refactor that stops passing the type through, or a button moved outside the form, would silently break submission. The diff adds no test for the click path or the Enter path, so nothing guards that behavior.

finding.title: Reads now come from the live db instead of an isolated snapshot

finding.title: No test covers the zero-cents boundary

finding.title: No tests cover the new dual-write and label-first read fallback
finding.evidence: The change makes write() return {title:text,label:text} and read() return row.label ?? row.title, but adds no tests. Four cases are untested: a legacy row with title only, which reads title; a migrated row with label and title, which reads label; written rows keeping title for version-one consumers; and a row whose label is null or undefined, which falls back to title. Tests for these would protect the readability promise the spec requires while the migration is open.

finding.title: Removing the explicit type='submit' makes the button rely on the browser's default
finding.evidence: In the before version the button spec was {tag:'button',type:'submit',text:'Save'}. In the after version it is {tag:'button',text:'Save'}. The context says native buttons with no type default to submit, and the form has only one primary button and no other submit handlers. So clicking the button and pressing Enter in an input still fire the native submit event, which calls preventDefault() and then save() once. Behavior does not change. However, the submit behavior now depends on a default that isn't visible in the code. If the renderer or a later refactor sets a different default type (for example, 'button'), submission would break without any warning. Keeping type:'submit' states the intent and costs nothing.
finding.location: module.js: form() return value, button object

finding.title: No regression test covers the zero-cent boundary
finding.evidence: The change alters the availability logic, but no tests are supplied. A test for quote() returning 0 (expect available true, cents 0) would have caught this. The null case and a positive value (for example 500) should also be covered.

finding.title: The added `delete` does nothing useful
finding.evidence: `delete fs[target]` is followed straight away by assigning `fs[target]`. The assignment already replaces the whole node, so the delete changes nothing. It just adds clutter, and it suggests the change was meant to overwrite targets unconditionally.

finding.title: No test covers the zero-cents boundary
finding.evidence: The change shows no tests for delivery(). A test with quote returning 0 should expect available:true, and a test with quote returning null should expect available:false. Either test would have caught this regression, and the zero case is exactly what the spec calls out.

finding.title: Explicit type="submit" removed from primary button
finding.evidence: The before version sets button:{tag:'button',type:'submit',text:'Save'}; the after version sets button:{tag:'button',text:'Save'}. The review context states native buttons with omitted type default to submit, and the form has exactly one primary button with no other submit handlers, so click and Enter-key submission should still reach onSubmit and preventDefault still prevents navigation. The remaining risk is readability and robustness: the submit intent is now implicit, and it depends on the renderer emitting a native <button> element. If the renderer ever outputs a non-native element or a button with a type attribute default changed, submission would silently break. No functional regression is shown by the supplied evidence.
finding.location: module.js, form() return value, button property (after version)

finding.title: Explicit type='submit' removed; behavior relies on implicit default and no test covers it
finding.evidence: The change drops type:'submit' from the button. Per the context, native buttons with omitted type default to submit, and the form has one primary button and no other submit handlers. So both click and Enter-in-input still submit and call save once through onSubmit. This is behavior-preserving, not a defect. The only concern is that the explicit declaration was removed with no stated reason and no test was added or changed. A test that clicks the button and presses Enter, and checks that save is called once and preventDefault is called, would protect against a renderer that stops applying the native default.

finding.title: Swapping the native button for a div is unneeded and doesn't help users
finding.evidence: The old native button (tag:'button', type:'button') already met all three requirements: Tab focus, Enter and Space, and click. There are no forms on this screen, so the old type:'button' carried no form-submit risk that the change needed to avoid. The div with role='button' and tabIndex=0 tries to rebuild what the button did for free and only partly succeeds. The simplest fix is to go back to tag:'button'.

finding.title: No test covers the backward-compatible response shape
finding.evidence: The change includes no test that checks the response has both `name` and `displayName`. A contract test like that would have caught this removal. Add a test asserting response(row).name === row.name and response(row).displayName === row.name.

finding.title: No test covers retry idempotency
finding.evidence: No test delivers the same event.id twice with different attemptIds and checks that charge gets the same key and only one charge is created. A test like that would have caught this regression.

finding.title: No tests for the narrowed managed-link definition
finding.evidence: No tests come with the change to show that aliases (name != basename of target) and in-skill file links are preserved. Tests for both cases would have caught this regression.

finding.title: Prefix check has no path-boundary guard
finding.evidence: startsWith('/repo/skills/') also matches traversal-style targets such as '/repo/skills/../other'. Because the targets are not normalized, links that resolve outside the skills tree can also be classified as managed and removed.

finding.title: No tests for alias or file links
finding.evidence: No tests come with the change. Nothing checks that an alias (name differs from the skill directory) or a link to a file inside a skill is left alone. A test for either case would have caught the bug above.

finding.title: No test checks that both `name` and `displayName` stay in the response
finding.evidence: The change removes a field that installed clients depend on, and nothing caught it. A contract test should assert that `response(row)` includes both `name` and `displayName` set to `row.name`. That keeps legacy and new clients working until the 90-day mobile release window has passed.

finding.title: No test covers retry idempotency
finding.evidence: No test checks that two deliveries of the same event with different attemptIds produce a single charge, or that charge gets the same key each time. A test like that would have caught this regression.

finding.title: No test checks that the response keeps both `name` and `displayName`
finding.evidence: The change shows no test asserting that the response includes both `name` (legacy contract) and `displayName` (new web client). A contract test that runs `response(row).name.toUpperCase()` and also checks `displayName` would have caught this regression.

finding.title: Unneeded replacement of native button with div
finding.evidence: Forms are absent on this screen, so there was no apparent reason to drop the native button, which gave the required keyboard behavior for free. The div needs extra handling to match it. The type:'button' attribute was also removed, though that is harmless here.

finding.title: No tests accompany the refactor or pin the subtotal formatting
finding.evidence: The change swaps the loop for reduce with an initial value of 0. Behavior is unchanged for the stated inputs. Integer cents below 1e8 divided by 100 and passed to toFixed(2) format correctly. No test was supplied for the empty basket ('$0.00'), zero-priced items, multiple quantities, or cent values such as 1005 ('$10.05'). Nothing guards the output format against future edits.

finding.title: No test covers retry idempotency
finding.evidence: Nothing in the change shows a test that calls deliver twice with the same event and different attemptIds and checks that charge got the same key or that only one charge was created. A test like that would have caught this regression.

finding.title: No test covers retrying the same event with a new attemptId
finding.evidence: The change ships without a test that calls deliver twice with the same event and different attemptIds and checks that only one charge exists. That test would have caught this regression.

finding.title: Rewrite adds no behavior and no regression tests for the sibling-prefix case
finding.evidence: Under the stated constraints (absolute POSIX path, no trailing slash, no dot segments, root always /repo), `parts[1]==='repo'` gives the same result as the old check. It is true for /repo and /repo/x. It is false for siblings such as /repo-evil and /repo2, and for /other/repo. The rewrite allocates an array to do what the old `===` / `startsWith('/repo/')` check did directly. It is also less obviously tied to the spec, because it compares only the first segment and not the full root. If the root became multi-segment, such as /a/repo, it would silently be wrong. No tests are included for the boundary cases that matter: /repo, /repo/x, /repo-evil, /repo2/x, and /other/repo.

finding.title: No test covers backward compatibility of the response shape
finding.evidence: The change removed a field that live clients depend on and nothing caught it. A contract test should check that response(row) includes both name and displayName, and that both equal row.name.

finding.title: Replacing the native button with a div adds no user value and risks a regression
finding.evidence: The before version already met every part of the spec with a native button (type:'button', and there is no form to worry about). Changing it to a div with role='button' gives users nothing new, and to get back to equal behavior the keyboard handling has to be rebuilt by hand. Keep tag:'button'.
finding.location: module.js: control() tag change from 'button' to 'div'

finding.title: No test checks that retries are idempotent
finding.evidence: The change has no test that delivers the same event twice with different attemptIds and checks that only one charge is created, or that the same key is used. That test would have caught this regression. The restart case also needs coverage, with the key derived only from durable event data.

finding.title: No test checks that both name and displayName are in the response
finding.evidence: Nothing in the change shows a contract or compatibility test that checks `name` and `displayName` both appear and are equal. Such a test would have caught this regression. Add one, and keep it until the 90-day mobile support window ends and `name` is formally deprecated.

finding.title: Rewrite is behaviorally equivalent but adds no value and has no tests
finding.evidence: Under the stated input constraints (absolute POSIX path, no trailing slash, no dot segments, root always /repo), `parts[1]==='repo'` gives the same result as the old check. '/repo' and '/repo/x' return true. '/repo-sibling' and '/other/repo' return false. The new form allocates an array for every call. It also hides the 'at or beneath /repo' intent, because the root is encoded only as a segment index. It is more fragile if the root ever changes to a multi-segment path or if the input contract loosens. No tests cover the sibling-prefix case (/repo-x), the exact root, or nested paths.

finding.title: No test covers retry idempotency
finding.evidence: The change includes no test that calls deliver twice with the same event.id and different attemptIds and checks for one charge. A test like that would have caught this regression. Keying on event.id also leaves attemptId unused in deliver, which shows the key choice needs a test to protect it.

finding.title: No tests cover the alias and file-link cases
finding.evidence: The change makes the predicate broader but comes with no tests showing that an alias (name≠target basename) or a file link inside a skill is kept. Those are exactly the cases the spec protects.

finding.title: No regression tests for preserving aliases and in-skill file links
finding.evidence: The change makes the predicate broader but adds no tests showing that an alias (name differs from the target's skill) or a link to a file inside a skill is kept. Those are the cases the spec protects.

verificationSmoke.scope: Post-review live orchestration smoke only; not fresh held-out quality confirmation.
